mainTopic: Confirming a שטר's signatures: רבי vs. the חכמים, אביי's clay-shard method, and שמואל's rulings on confirming documents
overview: The גמרא explains the argument between רבי and the חכמים about confirming a שטר. רבי holds that the signers testify about their handwriting, so each signature needs two witnesses. The חכמים hold that they testify about the money, so the two signers are enough. The גמרא shows that רבי was certain, not just unsure, so in one case he is lenient: a dead signer's signature needs only one outside witness, while the חכמים require two. If only one outside witness can be found, אביי suggests that the living signer write his signature on a clay shard so the court can confirm it, and then he and the outsider testify about the dead signer's signature. Parchment is not allowed for this, because a cheat could write a debt above the signature. שמואל rules like the חכמים, and the גמרא defends that report against a שטר from his own court, explaining it as extra care for orphans. Finally, שמואל's rule that a witness and a judge join together is attacked by רבא and rejected by רמי בר יחזקאל.

steps.title: What the witnesses are really testifying about
steps.stepSummary: According to רבי, the signers are testifying about their handwriting. According to the חכמים, they are testifying about the money in the שטר.
steps.simpleTranslation: According to רבי, they are testifying about their handwriting. According to the חכמים, they are testifying about the hundred-dinar sum written in the document.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the reason behind the argument between רבי and the חכמים about how a שטר gets confirmed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the testimony is about handwriting (רבי), each signer is only one witness for his own signature, so each signature needs a second witness. If the testimony is about the money (חכמים), the two signers together form a full pair of witnesses about the loan, and that is enough.

keyTerms.meaning: Their handwriting, meaning their own signatures
A sum of one hundred dinars; here, the loan amount in the document
A legal document, here a loan document

steps.whatToRemember: רבי: the testimony is about the signatures. חכמים: the testimony is about the money.

phrases.english: [According to רבי,] they are testifying about their handwriting.

phrases.aramaic: לְדִבְרֵי חֲכָמִים, עַל מָנֶה שֶׁבַּשְּׁטָר הֵם מְעִידִים.
phrases.english: According to the Sages, they are testifying about the hundred-dinar sum in the document.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the explanation of the argument between רבי and the חכמים, which began just before this section.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי sees the testimony as being about the signatures. The חכמים see it as being about the money in the שטר.

steps.title: Isn't that obvious?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why this explanation needs to be said at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: Isn't this obvious?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the explanation it just gave, saying it seems too obvious to need stating.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once we know that רבי requires two witnesses for each signature, it seems clear that he sees the testimony as being about handwriting. So what did the previous line add?

keyTerms.meaning: It is obvious; a challenge saying a statement adds nothing new

phrases.english: Isn't it obvious?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges whether Step 1 teaches anything new.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The explanation seems to follow automatically from רבי's known ruling, so it should not need to be stated.

steps.title: We might have thought רבי was only unsure
steps.stepSummary: The explanation is needed so we don't think רבי was in doubt about what the witnesses are testifying about.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have said that רבי was unsure whether they are testifying about their handwriting or about the hundred-dinar sum in the document.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the explanation teaches us that רבי was certain, not just unsure.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי's demand for two witnesses per signature could have been explained as a strict ruling made out of doubt. The explanation in Step 1 tells us that רבי clearly holds the testimony is about the handwriting.

keyTerms.meaning: You might have said; introduces a mistaken assumption that the teaching comes to correct
He is in doubt about it

steps.confusionAlert: Do not read this as the גמרא's conclusion. 'You might have said' is the mistaken idea, and the explanation in Step 1 comes to rule it out.

phrases.english: Lest you say
that רבי is uncertain about it

phrases.aramaic: אִי עַל כְּתַב יָדָם הֵם מְעִידִים,
phrases.english: whether they are testifying about their handwriting,

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ עַל מָנֶה שֶׁבַּשְּׁטָר הֵם מְעִידִים.
phrases.english: or they are testifying about the hundred-dinar sum in the document.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the 'isn't it obvious' challenge of Step 2.
steps.terutzResolutionType: The statement rules out a mistaken assumption
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי was only unsure, and he was strict out of doubt.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי is certain that the testimony is about the handwriting.

steps.title: The practical difference: one signer has died
steps.stepSummary: If רבי were only unsure, then when one signer dies we would need two outside witnesses to confirm the dead signer's signature.
steps.simpleTranslation: The practical difference is where one of them died: we would need two people from the street to testify about his signature.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows how it makes a real difference whether רבי was certain or only unsure.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If רבי is certain the testimony is about handwriting, the living signer plus one outsider can confirm the dead man's signature. If רבי were only unsure, we would have to worry that the testimony is about the money, and then two separate outsiders would be needed.

keyTerms.meaning: The practical difference that comes out of it
Two people from the street; outside witnesses who did not sign

phrases.english: And the practical difference
is where one of them died:

phrases.aramaic: לִבְעֵי שְׁנַיִם מִן הַשּׁוּק לְהָעִיד עָלָיו.
phrases.english: we would need two from the street to testify about him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the answer by showing a practical result of the 'unsure' approach.
steps.terutzResolutionType: A practical difference that shows the statement is needed
steps.terutzHavaAmina: If רבי were unsure, we would need two outside witnesses for the dead signer.
steps.terutzMaskana: Since רבי is certain, the living signer plus one outsider is enough.

steps.title: Why one outsider would not be enough if רבי were unsure
steps.stepSummary: If the testimony were about the money, three-quarters of the loan would be collected on the word of one witness.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because if so, the money minus a quarter would be collected on the word of one witness.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why, under the 'unsure' approach, the living signer could not be one of the witnesses for the dead man's signature.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the testimony is about the money, each witness counts for part of the sum. The living signer covers half through his own signature, and another quarter by sharing the dead man's half with the outsider. That makes him responsible for three-quarters of the money by himself, but money is collected only through two witnesses.

keyTerms.meaning: On the word (literally the mouth) of one witness

steps.whatToRemember: רבי is certain the signers testify about their handwriting. So a living signer plus one outsider can confirm a dead signer's signature, and there is no worry that most of the money rests on one witness.

phrases.english: For if so,
phrases.notes: "If so" means: if the testimony is about the money, and only one outsider joins the signer who is still alive.

phrases.english: the money, less a quarter, is collected
on the word of one witness.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reason for the rule stated in Step 4.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains the reasoning behind the practical difference
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Under the 'unsure' approach, one outsider would leave three-quarters of the money resting on one witness.
steps.terutzMaskana: The explanation in Step 1 shows רבי is certain, so this problem does not come up in his view.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows how 'what are the witnesses testifying about' decides real cases, like confirming a שטר after a signer has died.

steps.title: If רבי were unsure, he would be strict both ways
steps.stepSummary: This finishes the 'we might have thought' side. If רבי were in doubt, he would rule stringently in both cases.
steps.simpleTranslation: So here we would be strict, and here we would be strict.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא wraps up the mistaken idea from the last steps. If רבי were unsure, we would play it safe in both cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If both signers are alive, we would treat their testimony as being about the handwriting and add another witness. If one died, we would treat it as being about the money and require two outside witnesses. Doubt means being strict in both directions.

phrases.english: And here, stringently,
phrases.notes: This is the case where both signers are alive: add another witness, since maybe they testify about their handwriting.

phrases.english: and here, stringently.
phrases.notes: This is the case where one signer died: require two outside witnesses, since maybe they testify about the money.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the 'we would have thought' side begun in steps 3–5 by stating the result: strict in both cases.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Spelling out the mistaken idea that the statement prevents
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי was unsure, so he would be strict both when the signers are alive and when one died.
steps.terutzMaskana: This mistaken idea is what the statement comes to rule out.

steps.title: רבי was certain, so he rules both leniently and strictly
steps.stepSummary: The statement teaches that רבי was sure the signers testify about their handwriting. That certainty makes him lenient in one case and strict in the other.
steps.simpleTranslation: It teaches us that the matter was clear to רבי, which leads to both a lenient ruling and a strict ruling.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the real lesson of the earlier statement: רבי was not in doubt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because רבי is sure the testimony is about the handwriting, one outside witness is enough when a signer died. That is the lenient side. When both signers are alive, an additional witness is still needed. That is the strict side. Someone who was only in doubt would never end up lenient.

keyTerms.meaning: it teaches us (introduces the real point)
it was completely clear to him

steps.whatToRemember: רבי is certain that the signers testify about their handwriting. That is why he can be lenient in one case and strict in the other.

phrases.english: It teaches us
that it was entirely clear to Rabbi,
both leniently and stringently.

steps.triggerLanguage: קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן דְּרַבִּי מִיפְשָׁט פְּשִׁיטָא לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the mistaken idea (step 6) to the real lesson.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Answering 'why say it' by showing what it teaches
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי was unsure and would always be strict.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי was certain, so his rulings go both lenient and strict.

steps.title: רב shows where רבי is lenient
steps.stepSummary: רב rules that when one of two signers died, the חכמים require two outside witnesses for his signature, but רבי is lenient.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of רב: if two signed a שטר and one died, two people from outside are needed to confirm his signature. Here רבי is lenient and the חכמים are strict.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a statement of רב as support. It shows a case where רבי really is lenient.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If one signer dies, the חכמים require two outside witnesses, because they view the testimony as being about the money. רבי needs only one more witness, because he is sure the testimony is about the handwriting. This proves רבי was not in doubt, since doubt would never lead to a lenient ruling.

keyTerms.meaning: the ones signed on the document (the witnesses)

steps.whyThisMatters: This is the practical case where knowing whether רבי was certain or unsure changes the outcome.

phrases.english: As Rav Yehuda said that Rav said:
Two who are signed on a document
and one of them died —
they need two from the street
to testify about him,
in this case Rabbi is lenient,
and the Rabbis are strict.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Backs up step 7's claim that רבי has a lenient ruling.
steps.raayaObject: That רבי rules leniently in some case, showing he was certain.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רב יהודה in the name of רב: when one signer died, רבי is lenient and the חכמים are strict.

steps.title: What if only one outside witness is available?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how to confirm the שטר according to the strict view of the חכמים when only one outside witness exists.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if there are not two, but only one, what can be done?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a practical question. If we cannot find two outside witnesses, only one, is the שטר lost? This sets up אביי's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to the חכמים, the dead witness's signature needs two outside witnesses. The question is whether there is a workaround when only one is available.

phrases.english: And if there are not two
but only one, what?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי לֵיכָּא תְּרֵי אֶלָּא חַד, מַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on רב's case and asks about a harder situation.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How to confirm the שטר when only one outside witness is available.

steps.title: אביי's clay-shard method
steps.stepSummary: The living signer writes his signature on a clay shard for the court. The court confirms his signature by comparison, and he joins the outside witness to confirm the dead signer's signature.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: let him write his signature on a clay shard and toss it into the court. The court confirms his signature from it, so he does not need to testify about his own signature. Then he and the other witness go and testify about the other signature.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי gives a practical way to save the שטר with only one outside witness.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The court compares the shard to the שטר and confirms the living signer's signature itself. That leaves him free to serve as a witness. Together with the one outside witness, he makes two witnesses for the dead signer's signature, which satisfies even the חכמים.

phrases.english: Abaye said:
Let him write his signature on a clay shard,
phrases.notes: "He" is the signer who is still alive.

phrases.english: and toss it into the court,
and the court confirms it
(and they see it),
phrases.notes: These words in round brackets are in the printed גמרא, but some versions leave them out.

phrases.english: and he does not need
to testify about his own signature,
and he and this one go,
phrases.notes: "This one" is the single outside witness.

phrases.english: and testify about the other.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי לִכְתּוֹב חֲתִימַת יְדֵיהּ אַחַסְפָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 9.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The court confirms the living signer's signature by comparing it to the shard, so he and the outside witness can together confirm the dead signer's signature.

steps.title: Only on clay, never on parchment
steps.stepSummary: The sample signature must be written on a clay shard and not on parchment. Someone dishonest could find the parchment and write anything he wants above the signature.
steps.simpleTranslation: This applies specifically to a clay shard, but not to parchment. Maybe a dishonest person will find it and write on it whatever he wants.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a limit to אביי's method: use clay, not parchment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A loose signature on parchment is dangerous. A cheat could write a debt above it and make it look like a real IOU. A signature on clay cannot be misused this way.

phrases.english: And specifically on a clay shard,
but not on parchment,
since perhaps a person will find it
who is not honest
and write on it whatever he wants.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Qualifies אביי's method from step 10.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The sample signature for the court must be on clay, not parchment, to prevent forgery.

steps.title: A handwritten IOU can collect a debt
steps.stepSummary: A משנה teaches that a note in a person's own handwriting saying he owes money lets the lender collect from his unsold property. This shows the forgery risk is real.
steps.simpleTranslation: And we learned in a משנה: if someone produced a note in the other person's handwriting saying he owes him, the lender collects from free (unsold) property.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a משנה to show why parchment is dangerous. A forged note above a real signature could actually collect money.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A note in the borrower's own hand is enough to collect from his unsold property, even with no witnesses. So a cheat who writes a debt above a real signature on parchment could take real money. That is the reason for the clay-only rule.
steps.whatToRemember: אביי's clay shard solves the one-witness problem. Clay is required because a signature on parchment could be turned into a forged IOU that really collects.

phrases.english: And we learned:
If he produced against him his handwriting
that he owes him —
he collects from free property.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports step 11 by showing that a forged handwritten note would really work.
steps.raayaObject: That a signature on parchment poses a real forgery risk.
steps.raayaSupportSource: משנה: a note in the debtor's handwriting collects from unsold property.

steps.title: שמואל rules like the חכמים
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה quotes שמואל: the הלכה follows the חכמים in the dispute about confirming signatures on a שטר.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of שמואל: the הלכה follows the חכמים.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ruling. In the dispute between רבי and the חכמים about confirming a שטר, we follow the חכמים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The חכמים say each signer only has to vouch for his own signature, and the שטר is confirmed. רבי is stricter. שמואל decides the practical הלכה for the חכמים.

keyTerms.meaning: The majority of Sages in the משנה

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said that Shmuel said:
The halakha follows the words of the Rabbis.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל: הֲלָכָה כְּדִבְרֵי חֲכָמִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After discussing how to confirm the שטר, the גמרא now states which opinion is the practical הלכה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The הלכה follows the חכמים, not רבי.

steps.title: Why say it? The majority always wins
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that this ruling is obvious, because when one Sage argues with many, we follow the many.
steps.simpleTranslation: That's obvious! When one argues against many, the הלכה follows the many!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges שמואל's ruling as unnecessary. There is already a general rule that the majority wins.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי is one person and the חכמים are a group. The standard rule יחיד ורבים הלכה כרבים already gives us the answer. So why did שמואל need to say anything?

keyTerms.meaning: It's obvious! (an objection that a statement teaches nothing new)

phrases.english: It is obvious!
An individual against many — the halakha follows the many!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks step 13 as saying nothing new.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's ruling that the הלכה follows the חכמים
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The general majority rule already settles the question, so the ruling seems pointless.

steps.title: We might have thought רבי beats even a group
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that we might have thought רבי's special status lets him win even against many Sages. שמואל teaches that it does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have said: the הלכה follows רבי against one colleague, and even against several colleagues. So שמואל teaches us otherwise.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why שמואל's ruling is needed. There is a special rule that רבי usually wins his arguments, and we might have stretched it too far.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is a known rule that the הלכה follows רבי against a single colleague. Without שמואל, we might have applied that even when רבי argues with a group. שמואל teaches that in this case the majority still wins.

keyTerms.meaning: You might have said (introduces a mistaken idea)
The הלכה follows רבי against one colleague

steps.confusionAlert: Notice the difference: חֲבֵירוֹ is one colleague, and חֲבֵירָיו is several colleagues. The whole answer depends on that one letter י.

phrases.english: What might you have said?
The halakha follows Rabbi against his colleague,
and even against his colleagues;
so he teaches us.
phrases.notes: He teaches us that רבי's special rule only works against one colleague.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the פשיטא of step 14.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Shows the ruling is needed to block a mistaken extension of a different rule
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי's special status might let him win even against many Sages.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי's special status works only against one colleague, so here the חכמים win.

steps.title: Did שמואל really say that?
steps.stepSummary: After a memory aid for the names, a student (there are three versions of who) asks רב יהודה whether שמואל really ruled like the חכמים.
steps.simpleTranslation: A memory aid: נח, נד, חד. רב חיננא בר חייא said to רב יהודה (some say it was רב הונא בר יהודה, and some say רב חייא בר יהודה): Did שמואל really say this?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sets up a challenge to רב יהודה's report. It first gives a memory aid for three possible names of the challenger. The proof for the challenge comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The three letter-pairs match the first letters of each challenger's name and his father's name. The question 'ומי אמר שמואל הכי' doubts that שמואל ruled like the חכמים, and it prepares for the evidence that follows.

keyTerms.meaning: But did he really say...? (opens a challenge)

phrases.english: A mnemonic: Nun-Chet, Nun-Dalet, Chet-Dalet.
phrases.notes: נח is חִנָּנָא and חִיָּיא, נד is הוּנָא and יְהוּדָה, חד is חִיָּיא and יְהוּדָה. These are the three names that follow.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב חִנָּנָא בַּר חִיָּיא לְרַב יְהוּדָה,
phrases.english: Rav Chinnana bar Chiyya said to Rav Yehuda,

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמְרִי לַהּ רַב הוּנָא בַּר יְהוּדָה לְרַב יְהוּדָה,
phrases.english: and some say it was Rav Huna bar Yehuda to Rav Yehuda,

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמְרִי לַהּ רַב חִיָּיא בַּר יְהוּדָה לְרַב יְהוּדָה:
phrases.english: and some say it was Rav Chiyya bar Yehuda to Rav Yehuda:
And did Shmuel really say this?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to step 13 and questions whether שמואל really held this ruling.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב יהודה's report that שמואל ruled like the חכמים
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Sets up a contradiction from שמואל's own court practice, which is brought in the next step.

steps.title: The שטר from שמואל's own court
steps.stepSummary: A שטר from שמואל's court records that each of the two signers vouched for his own signature and also for his partner's. That is what רבי requires.
steps.simpleTranslation: But there was a שטר that came out of שמואל's court, and it said: 'Since רב ענן בר חייא came and testified about his own signature and about his partner's, רב חנן בר רבה, and since רב חנן בר רבה came and testified about his own signature and about his partner's, רב ענן בר חייא, we confirmed and approved it properly.'
steps.whatsHappening: This is the evidence behind the challenge. In שמואל's own court, each signer was made to vouch for both signatures.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to the חכמים, it should be enough for each signer to vouch only for his own signature. שמואל's court had each one vouch for both, which fits רבי's stricter view. So it looks like שמואל actually followed רבי.

keyTerms.meaning: We certified and confirmed it (the court's approval formula)

phrases.english: But wasn't there that document
that came out of the court of Mar Shmuel,
and it was written in it:
Since Rav Anan bar Chiyya came
and testified about his own signature
and about the one who signed with him,
and who is he — Rav Chanan bar Rabba;
and since Rav Chanan bar Rabba came
and testified about his own signature
and about the one who signed with him,
and who is he — Rav Anan bar Chiyya;
we certified and confirmed it as is proper?
phrases.notes: The point is that if שמואל followed the חכמים, there was no need for each signer to vouch for the other's signature.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָא הָהוּא שְׁטָרָא דִּנְפַק מִבֵּי דִינָא דְּמָר שְׁמוּאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the evidence for the challenge in step 16.
steps.raayaObject: That שמואל did not rule like the חכמים
steps.raayaSupportSource: An actual שטר confirmed in שמואל's court, where each signer vouched for both signatures
steps.kashyaTarget: רב יהודה's report (step 13) that שמואל ruled like the חכמים
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: In שמואל's own court, each signer testified about both his own signature and his partner's signature. If שמואל held like the חכמים, testifying to his own signature would have been enough, so his court's practice looks like רבי's view.

steps.title: It was an orphans' שטר
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה answers that the שטר belonged to orphans, and שמואל worried that some court might rule wrongly against them.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: That was an orphans' שטר, and שמואל was worried about a court that might make a mistake.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה defends his report. That case was special because it involved orphans.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל still holds like the חכמים. But because this שטר belonged to orphans, he was extra careful, in case a later בית דין rejected the שטר by mistake.

keyTerms.meaning: A court that makes a mistake

phrases.english: He said to him:
That was a document of orphans,
and Shmuel was concerned about a court that errs.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: הָהוּא שְׁטָרָא דְיַתְמֵי הֲוָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of steps 16-17 by showing the case was special.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: שמואל's court practice shows he follows רבי.
steps.terutzMaskana: שמואל follows the חכמים. He only did extra for orphans, out of fear of a mistaken court.

steps.title: Doing extra so the orphans won't lose
steps.stepSummary: The answer goes on: שמואל feared a court might think רבי wins even against a group in this case, so he confirmed the שטר in a way that satisfies everyone.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל thought: maybe someone holds that the הלכה follows רבי against one colleague but not against several, and yet in this case even against several. So he said: I will be generous, so the orphans do not lose.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes רב יהודה's answer. It explains exactly which mistake שמואל was worried about, and why he went beyond the basic law.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Some court might make an exception and follow רבי here even against the majority, and then reject a שטר confirmed only by the חכמים' method. To protect the orphans, שמואל confirmed it in a way that works under both views. His basic ruling stays like the חכמים.

keyTerms.meaning: Extra room, doing more than needed

steps.whatToRemember: שמואל rules like the חכמים: each signer only needs to vouch for his own signature. In an orphans' case he went further and satisfied רבי too, so that no court could reject the שטר.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that a court's extra caution in one special case does not prove its basic ruling. We have to ask whether it was the basic law or extra protection.

phrases.english: And Shmuel thought:
perhaps there is someone who holds:
the halakha follows Rabbi against his colleague but not against his colleagues,
and in this case even against his colleagues,
he thought: I will do it in a generous way
so that the orphans will not lose.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּסְבַר שְׁמוּאֵל דִּלְמָא אִיכָּא דִּסְבִירָא לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Spells out the reasoning behind step 18's concern about a mistaken court.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains the precaution so it satisfies all views
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Confirming the שטר in רבי's way shows that the הלכה follows רבי.
steps.terutzMaskana: It was only a precaution against a court that might follow רבי here. The basic הלכה follows the חכמים.

steps.title: A witness and a judge can join together
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה reports that שמואל ruled that a witness and a judge can combine to make a pair of witnesses.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of שמואל: A witness and a judge join together.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ruling from שמואל: one witness who signed a שטר and one judge who confirmed it can count together as two.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The case is a שטר that a court already confirmed, and now the borrower says it is forged. Normally we need two people to back up the שטר. שמואל says one signing witness plus one judge from the confirming court is enough.

keyTerms.meaning: A witness (here, one who signed the שטר)
A judge (here, one who sat on the court that confirmed the שטר)
They join together, they count as a pair

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said that Shmuel said:
A witness and a judge join together.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל: עֵד וְדַיָּין מִצְטָרְפִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new ruling from שמואל about confirming שטרות, after the earlier discussion of how שמואל confirmed the orphans' שטר.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One signing witness and one confirming judge combine to back up a שטר.

steps.title: רמי בר חמא praises the ruling
steps.stepSummary: רמי בר חמא says שמואל's ruling is an excellent one.
steps.simpleTranslation: רמי בר חמא said: How excellent is this teaching!
steps.whatsHappening: רמי בר חמא praises שמואל's ruling. This sets up the next step, where רבא questions what is so good about it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The praise adds no new law. It shows that the ruling was taken seriously, which makes רבא's attack in the next step stand out.

keyTerms.meaning: A teaching, a ruling that was heard and passed on

phrases.english: Rami bar Ḥama said:
How excellent is this teaching!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds to שמואל's ruling with approval.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רמי בר חמא approves of the rule that a witness and a judge join together.

steps.title: רבא: they are testifying about different things
steps.stepSummary: רבא challenges the ruling: the witness and the judge each testify about a different fact, so neither fact has two witnesses.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: What is excellent about it? What the witness testifies about, the judge does not testify about. And what the judge testifies about, the witness does not testify about!
steps.whatsHappening: רבא attacks the ruling that רמי בר חמא just praised. He says a witness and a judge cannot really add up to two.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The witness testifies that he signed and saw the loan happen. The judge testifies that the court confirmed the שטר. Since they are talking about two different facts, each fact has only one witness, and one witness is not enough.

keyTerms.meaning: Excellence, what is good about it

steps.confusionAlert: רבא is not saying a judge can never be believed. He is saying the two people are not backing up the same fact, so they are not a real pair.

phrases.english: Rava said: What is excellent about it?
What the witness testifies about
the judge does not testify about,
and what the judge testifies about
the witness does not testify about!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the praise in step 21 and the ruling in step 20.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's rule that a witness and a judge join together.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Two witnesses must testify to the same fact. Here the witness backs the signing and the loan, and the judge backs the court's confirmation, so each fact has only one witness.

steps.title: רמי בר יחזקאל: do not rely on these rules
steps.stepSummary: רמי בר יחזקאל, רב יהודה's brother, says not to listen to the rules רב יהודה reported in שמואל's name.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, when רמי בר יחזקאל came, he said: Do not listen to those rules that my brother יהודה laid down in the name of שמואל.
steps.whatsHappening: The ruling from step 20 is pushed aside. רמי בר יחזקאל says his brother's reports of שמואל's rules should not be relied on.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word אלא shows that the גמרא accepts רבא's attack and drops the ruling. רמי בר יחזקאל does not argue the logic. He attacks the report itself: these rules should not be followed as שמואל's teaching.

keyTerms.meaning: That he laid down as a rule

steps.whatToRemember: שמואל's rule that a witness and a judge join together, as reported by רב יהודה, is challenged by רבא and then rejected by רמי בר יחזקאל.

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא כִּי אֲתָא רָמֵי בַּר יְחֶזְקֵאל, אָמַר:
phrases.english: Rather, when Rami bar Yeḥezkel came, he said:
Do not listen to those rules
that my brother Yehuda laid down in the name of Shmuel.
phrases.notes: "Yehuda" is רב יהודה, who reported the rule in step 20. He and רמי בר יחזקאל were brothers.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא כִּי אֲתָא רָמֵי בַּר יְחֶזְקֵאל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows רבא's attack by dropping the ruling entirely.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The whole rule that a witness and a judge join together, and the rules רב יהודה reported from שמואל on this topic.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The report of שמואל's ruling should not be relied on, and logically the two people do not testify to the same fact (step 22).
